tagline.text: A mountain garden above Davao, cooled by pine-forest breezes

location.label: Location
location.text: Eden, Toril District, Davao City, Davao del Sur

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to 2 days, 1 night

image.credit: Michael E. Peligro / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A mountain resort about an hour's drive from downtown Davao, set at about 900m above sea level on the slopes of Mount Talomo. In a pine forest replanted over decades on land once stripped bare by logging, you can enjoy cool air, flower gardens, a zipline, and an organic-vegetable buffet.
Eden Nature Park and Resort is a mountain nature park and resort in Barangay Eden, Toril District, in the southwest of Davao City, set at about
(roughly 3,000 feet) above sea level on the slopes of Mount Talomo. It's about
30km
from the city center, reachable in around
1 hour
by car, and the air changes noticeably as you climb, with cool breezes around
even at midday. Escaping the hot Davao city center for just half a day can feel like arriving in Baguio or Tagaytay, and the park has long been a beloved weekend outing spot for locals.
What makes this place special is that most of its scenery is a forest brought back to life by human hands. When founders Jesus V. Ayala and his wife first came upon this land in
, it was a wasteland stripped bare by illegal logging and overgrown with only wild grass. After decades of planting and tending saplings, it now forms a dense forest of
over 100,000 pine trees
and tropical trees, with about 40 of its roughly 80 hectares developed into gardens and facilities. It's often cited as one of the Philippines' leading examples of private forest restoration.

Scattered around the park are flower and herb gardens, terraced vegetable plots, a deer pasture, Tinubdan, a space recreating indigenous culture, an outdoor amphitheater, a fishing pond, and a swimming pool. There are also thrill attractions such as the Skyrider zipline crossing above the pine forest, the Skycycle for pedaling a bike suspended high up, and the Skyswing that swings widely through the air, making the park popular with families, couples, and groups alike.

It suits travelers who want cool mountain air and green scenery without a rough hike or a long journey, families with children, and anyone who wants a day of rest between stretches of a Davao city itinerary. Most visitors come as a day trip, but staying overnight in a mountain cottage lets you enjoy a misty morning forest and a quiet walk.
A narrated tour on the park's own shuttle, taking about
45 minutes

around the main gardens, viewpoints, vegetable plots, and Tinubdan. The grounds are large and hilly, so first-time visitors do well to get their bearings on the shuttle, then walk back to the spots they liked.
Eden's signature attraction: glide across a cable about
long, suspended above the pine forest. The speed isn't fast, so it's approachable for first-timers and teens, and forest and valley unfold below your feet.

The Skycycle, where you pedal a bike across a wire suspended in the air, and the Skyswing, which swings widely at about 95 feet up, are popular with travelers after a thrill. There are height, weight, and health restrictions, so check the on-site guidance.

Take a slow walk along the pine-forest trails and flower gardens scattered through the park. The forest is especially photogenic early in the morning when low mist settles in, and the high elevation means you'll sweat less even while walking.

A cultural space recreating the traditional houses, everyday tools, and crafts of Mindanao's indigenous Lumad peoples. It offers a brief window into the stories of the various tribes living around Davao, making it a good educational stop for children too.

The park runs a farm that takes advantage of the highland climate to grow vegetables and herbs, and produce from it appears in the park restaurant's lunch buffet. You can enjoy fresh salads and Filipino home cooking with mountain views.
There's a short horseback-riding course suitable for children and beginners, and a fishing pond where they'll cook whatever you catch. Both are well suited to family travelers spending a relaxed day.

Direct flights from Manila to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO) take about
1 hour 50 minutes
, and about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Cebu. One-way fares run around
The airport is in the north of Davao City, while Eden sits at the southwestern edge, so it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes–2 hours
by car from the airport to Eden. Rather than heading straight there on arrival day, it's more convenient to stay overnight in the city and set out the next morning.
From downtown Davao it takes about
1 hour
by taxi or Grab, with one-way fares around
depending on traffic. Taxis back from the park to the city are hard to flag down, so it's safer to negotiate a round trip or a waiting arrangement.
If you're in a group, the most convenient option is to charter a van or car for the day (about
) and combine Eden with other city sights.

The park has at times run a shuttle from its office near Matina Town Square in the Matina area of the city. It generally departed in the morning and returned in the afternoon, mainly on weekends, but the fare and whether it's running change often, so check the park office or its official social media for the latest notices.
Budget travelers can take a jeepney to Toril from the city (about
), then continue up the mountain road toward Eden by jeepney or habal-habal (motorbike taxi, about
). It takes about
30–40 minutes
from Toril to the park.
Transport on the final stretch of mountain road thins out late in the afternoon. It's best to leave the park before
4 PM
on your way back.

Davao lies south of the typical Philippine typhoon path, so typhoon damage is rare, and rain falls fairly evenly year-round without a clearly defined dry or wet season. Eden can be visited any time of year, but
January–May
, with relatively more clear days, is best for walking and using the attractions.
June–December
sees frequent afternoon showers and mist, so it's best to arrive early in the morning and finish your outdoor plans first.
At about
above sea level, daytime temperatures run around
, some 5–8 degrees cooler than the city, and it can feel chilly in the early morning and at night. If staying overnight, bring a light long-sleeve shirt or windbreaker.
December
sometimes brings year-end light displays and events, and around the third week of
August
, when Davao's biggest festival, Kadayawan, is held, as well as Holy Week and the year-end holidays, the park gets crowded and rooms fill up fast.

Inside the park are cottages and lodge-style rooms set among the pine trees, with doubles running about
a night and family rooms for four around

. Many packages include breakfast and pool access, and the nights stay cool enough to rest without air conditioning, listening to the forest. Rooms fill up quickly on weekends and holidays due to group events, so book with the park office in advance. For a cheaper trip, the usual approach is to stay in downtown Davao (the Poblacion, Matina, and Lampudo areas) and visit as a day trip.
For a family gathering or a group, you can rent a whole house that sleeps 5–25 people together, such as Mountain Villa, Pine Lodge, Log Cabin, and Shangri-La. Rates run about
per night (room only, breakfast extra), and split among the group it can even work out cheaper than regular rooms.

The main meal is the lunch buffet at the park restaurant. It features salads and soups made from lettuce, herbs, and vegetables grown on the park's own farm, along with Filipino-style chicken and pork dishes, and choosing an entrance package that includes the buffet means you won't need to find a separate restaurant. Tilapia caught at the fishing pond can also be grilled or fried for you. Back in the city in the evening, be sure to try Davao's famous tuna dishes and tropical fruits like durian, mangosteen, and pomelo.
The park's operating hours are generally
8 AM–5 PM
. If you arrive when it opens, the lines at the activity facilities are short and you can also see the fog-covered forest scenery.
Activity facilities such as Skyrider, Skycycle, and Sky Swing operate only
1–5 PM
Monday to Thursday and
8 AM–5 PM
Friday to Sunday. All activities require signing a waiver, and minors need a guardian's consent. The latest price list is available on the
official website

Entrance tickets come in different packages depending on whether the lunch buffet or shuttle tour is included. Fares and packages change often, so check the official website or call the office before you visit.
The grounds are large with many uphill sections. Wear comfortable walking shoes, and pace yourself by taking the shuttle tour first before exploring on foot.
It's much cooler up the mountain than in the city, and afternoon rain is common. Bring a light jacket and an umbrella or raincoat.
Transport back is the biggest wildcard. If you arrive by taxi, arrange a waiting or pickup time with the driver in advance, or get their contact number.
There's a small shop and souvenir store inside the park, but they mainly take cash. Withdraw plenty of cash from an ATM as you pass through Toril.

If you want to combine this with the Philippine Eagle Center, note that the two sit on opposite sides of the city, southwest and northwest, so it's more relaxed to split them over two days rather than fit both into one.

Attractions such as the Skyswing and Skyrider have height, weight, age, and health restrictions. Those with heart conditions or high blood pressure, and pregnant visitors, should not use them, and operation may be suspended on days with strong wind and rain.
During the rainy season, forest trails and steps get slippery with moss and mud. Wear sturdy-soled shoes rather than sandals.
The mountain road up from Toril to the park has many curves and few streetlights. If riding a motorbike taxi or driving yourself, finish the trip before dark.
Don't feed the animals at the deer pasture human food or enter inside the fence.
At this elevation, the sun may seem mild but UV exposure is strong. Bring a hat and sunscreen.
Weekends and holidays bring a crush of group events and school trips, lengthening wait times at the attractions. For a quieter visit, come on a weekday morning.
